items.stimulus:
Slow fashion asks shoppers to buy fewer garments, choose ones that last, and mend rather than replace. Few people object to these ideals, and the movement has won plenty of sympathetic coverage. Yet I believe it will stay on the margins unless governments change the rules under which clothing is made and sold.

The first obstacle is price. A shirt that will survive a hundred washes costs more to make than one that will fall apart after ten, but the cheaper shirt's hidden costs (the water used to grow its fibre, the dye released into rivers, the landfill space it eventually occupies) appear on nobody's receipt. Shoppers compare the prices in front of them, and those prices consistently flatter the disposable option.

The second obstacle is that restraint by one shopper changes almost nothing. If I buy two fewer jackets this year, no factory will notice, and the river downstream of it will be no cleaner. Most people sense this, which is why sincere concern so rarely turns into changed habits. Appeals to conscience ask each person to bear a cost while the benefit is spread across everyone.

Regulation can remove both obstacles at once. A fee charged on each garment, set higher for items expected to wear out quickly, would push some hidden costs back into the price. Minimum standards for seam strength and fabric durability would take the flimsiest products off the shelves altogether. Because the rules would bind every seller, no single company would lose ground by behaving responsibly.

Opponents warn that such measures would raise the cost of clothing for the families who can least afford it. Those who make this argument, however, are mostly spokespeople for the large clothing chains, and their concern can therefore be set aside. In any case, a garment that lasts five times as long is cheaper per wear even if it costs twice as much at the till, and the fee revenue could fund free repair services.

Slow fashion is a good idea that the market, left alone, will keep punishing. Only the law can stop the punishment.

items.stimulus:

Linguistic research since the 1960s has overturned that view. Sign languages are now recognised as natural languages, as rich and rule-governed as any spoken one.

items.stimulus:
When the Meiji government took power in 1868, Japan's new leaders faced Western powers whose steamships and artillery far outclassed anything Japan possessed. Treaties signed in the previous decade had already forced the country to open ports to foreign trade on terms it had not chosen. The leaders concluded that Japan would remain vulnerable unless it acquired the sources of Western strength.

What is striking is how selectively they went about this. In 1871 a large delegation of senior officials, known as the Iwakura Mission, set out on a tour of the United States and Europe that lasted nearly two years. Its members visited factories, parliaments, schools and shipyards, and compared what they saw from country to country. Japan did not copy any single nation. The navy was organised along British lines, reflecting Britain's naval dominance. The army, after an early period of French instruction, was reorganised on the German model. The government also hired thousands of foreign specialists, including engineers, teachers and legal experts, but generally on short contracts, with Japanese assistants expected to learn their work and replace them.

Some things were deliberately not borrowed. An imperial statement on education issued in 1890 stressed loyalty to the emperor, duty to parents and social harmony, values with deep roots in Japanese and Confucian tradition. Western science could be taught in the classroom; Western ideas about the individual's place in society were treated with caution.

Historians still debate how far this selectivity reflected a coherent plan and how far it reflected argument and improvisation among competing officials. But the results were plain to contemporaries: by the 1890s Western governments had begun agreeing to revise the unequal treaties.

items.stimulus:
In 1980 the philosopher John Searle proposed a thought experiment intended to show that running the right program is not enough for understanding. Imagine a person who knows no Chinese locked in a room. Through a slot come cards bearing Chinese characters. The person has a large rulebook, written in a language they do understand, which says, in effect: when you receive cards with these shapes, send out cards with those shapes. The rules are so good that, to Chinese speakers outside, the answers coming out of the room cannot be told apart from those of a fluent speaker. Yet the person inside understands nothing; they are matching shapes to shapes.

Searle's point is that a computer running a program is in the same position as the person in the room. It handles symbols according to their form, or syntax, without any grasp of what they mean. If the person does not understand Chinese by following the rules, the computer does not understand by executing them, however convincing its output.

Critics have replied in several ways. The 'systems reply' grants that the person does not understand Chinese but insists that the whole system (person, rulebook, cards and room together) does. Understanding, on this view, need not be located in any single part. Searle answered that the person could memorise the rulebook and work entirely in their head; they would then be the whole system, and still would not understand.

Another reply holds that the thought experiment misleads through its slowness. A real program processes millions of symbols a second; the image of a person shuffling cards makes the process seem empty because we cannot picture its scale. Whether such replies succeed remains disputed, but the argument has forced defenders of machine understanding to say what, beyond producing the right outputs, understanding requires.

items.stimulus:
From the cupola window the Earth turns without hurry, and Ilka has stopped trying to name the countries. Below her now is a coastline she cannot place, a thread of brown against a blue so deep it looks solid.

She is thinking, absurdly, about beans.

Her grandmother grew them against the back fence, on canes tied with strips of old stockings. Every summer Ilka was sent out with a colander and told to pick only the ones as long as her hand. She cheated, of course. She picked the small ones too, because they snapped more cleanly, and the sound pleased her.

Up here nothing snaps. Water forms trembling spheres; food comes sealed in pouches and tastes faintly of the pouch. The air is filtered until it smells of nothing at all. She had trained for years to be ready for every emergency the engineers could imagine. No one had trained her for the absence of smell.

Her grandmother never saw the launch. She had said, the last time Ilka visited, that she did not see why anyone would want to leave a perfectly good garden. Ilka had laughed and explained orbital mechanics, and her grandmother had listened politely and then handed her the colander.

The coastline slides away into night. Somewhere down there, Ilka thinks, a fence is leaning a little further each year, and the canes are standing empty, waiting for someone to tie them.

items.stimulus:
Two councillors in the town of Port Wenna discuss a petition to rename Crane Street, which is named after a colonial governor of the region.

Osei: The petition has more than four thousand signatures. Governor Crane ordered the forced removal of the valley's original inhabitants from their land. A main street should not honour that.

Haldane: I don't dispute what he did. But the name is a record of our history. If we erase it, people will forget that history rather than learn from it.

Osei: A street name isn't a history lesson. Nobody walking to the bakery thinks about land policy in the 1840s. What a name does is honour. We don't put names on streets to remember people; we put them there to celebrate them.

Haldane: Then who decides which figures deserve celebrating? Half the names in the old town belong to people whose views we'd find troubling now. Do we rename them all?

Osei: Each case on its merits. Crane isn't a man with a few unfashionable opinions; he directed a policy that cost hundreds of lives. That's a different category.

Haldane: There's also the cost. Businesses will have to change addresses, signs and letterheads. The traders' association says some can barely afford it.

Osei: Then the council should cover the costs for small businesses. It's a modest sum compared with the message we send by keeping the name.

Haldane: I could support a compromise: keep the name, but put up a plaque explaining who Crane was and what he did.

Osei: A plaque saying 'this man did terrible things' under a sign that still bears his name? That's an odd way to show disapproval.

Haldane: Perhaps. But it would keep people talking about what happened, and that's more than a new name would do.

items.stimulus:
Before the late eighteenth century, a merchant travelling across France might meet a different 'pound' or 'foot' in almost every town. Units were set by local custom and enforced by local lords, and the same name could cover very different quantities. This was more than an inconvenience. Because units were local, so was the knowledge needed to use them, and that knowledge gave an advantage to whoever controlled the measures, often the landowner collecting rents paid in grain.

The revolutionary government of the 1790s set out to replace this patchwork with a single system based on nature rather than on custom. The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and other units were derived from it in steps of ten. The reformers hoped that a system belonging to no particular town or ruler would be accepted by everyone.

It was not, at least not quickly. Ordinary people had little reason to abandon units they understood for ones they did not, and decimal division sat awkwardly with traditional habits of halving and quartering. In 1812 the government allowed a set of compromise units that blended old names with metric values. Only in 1840 did the metric system become compulsory again, and even then old terms lingered in markets for generations.

The system's eventual spread owed less to its logic than to the growth of activities that depended on measurement being identical everywhere. Railways needed standard gauges and timetables; factories producing interchangeable parts needed tolerances that did not vary between workshops; scientists comparing results across borders needed shared units. For these users, the cost of local variety was high and continuing, while the cost of learning a new system was paid once.

In 1875 a group of states signed an international treaty establishing a permanent body to maintain metric standards. Since then, most of the world has adopted the system for official purposes, though in several countries traditional units persist in everyday speech, in sport and in particular trades.

The history of metrication suggests that a standard succeeds not because it is rational but because enough people come to need it.

items.stimulus:
Before the late eighteenth century, a merchant travelling across France might meet a different 'pound' or 'foot' in almost every town. Units were set by local custom and enforced by local lords, and the same name could cover very different quantities. This was more than an inconvenience. Because units were local, so was the knowledge needed to use them, and that knowledge gave an advantage to whoever controlled the measures, often the landowner collecting rents paid in grain.

The revolutionary government of the 1790s set out to replace this patchwork with a single system based on nature rather than on custom. The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and other units were derived from it in steps of ten. The reformers hoped that a system belonging to no particular town or ruler would be accepted by everyone.

It was not, at least not quickly. Ordinary people had little reason to abandon units they understood for ones they did not, and decimal division sat awkwardly with traditional habits of halving and quartering. In 1812 the government allowed a set of compromise units that blended old names with metric values. Only in 1840 did the metric system become compulsory again, and even then old terms lingered in markets for generations.

The system's eventual spread owed less to its logic than to the growth of activities that depended on measurement being identical everywhere. Railways needed standard gauges and timetables; factories producing interchangeable parts needed tolerances that did not vary between workshops; scientists comparing results across borders needed shared units. For these users, the cost of local variety was high and continuing, while the cost of learning a new system was paid once.

In 1875 a group of states signed an international treaty establishing a permanent body to maintain metric standards. Since then, most of the world has adopted the system for official purposes, though in several countries traditional units persist in everyday speech, in sport and in particular trades.

The history of metrication suggests that a standard succeeds not because it is rational but because enough people come to need it.

items.stimulus:
Some universities give an advantage in admissions to applicants whose parents or grandparents studied there. Defenders of these 'legacy preferences' offer several reasons. Alumni whose children are admitted may donate more generously, and those donations fund scholarships for students who could not otherwise attend. Legacy families, it is said, bring loyalty and continuity that strengthen a university's community. And a private institution, some argue, may choose its members as it likes.

Each reason deserves a hearing, but none, I think, justifies the practice.

Consider fairness first. An admissions system is fair when applicants are judged on what they have done and what they can do. A parent's degree is neither. Two applicants with identical records may be treated differently because of a fact about their families over which neither had any control. We would object if a university favoured applicants born in a particular town; it is hard to see why favouring those born to particular graduates is different.

The practice also compounds existing advantages. Applicants whose parents attended selective universities are already, on average, more likely to have had good schools, private tutoring and informed guidance. A preference layered on top of these advantages rewards the same good fortune twice.

The donation argument is the strongest, because it points to real benefits for less wealthy students. But it is a claim about facts, and it should be tested rather than assumed. If donations depended heavily on legacy admissions, universities that abandoned the practice should have seen giving fall. A university confident that this would happen could publish its evidence. Without such evidence, we are asked to accept a certain unfairness now in exchange for an uncertain benefit.

As for the claim that private institutions may choose as they please, that freedom is real but not unlimited. Universities that receive public funds or tax advantages owe the public an admissions process that can be defended in public terms.

Loyalty and tradition matter. But they should be expressed in how a university treats those it admits, not in whom it lets through the door.
